title: Great Seljuk Persia
subtitle: 1055–1219 · Tughril Beg to the Khwarazmian Twilight

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Tughril Beg's sultanate, Nizam al-Mulk's vizierate, fragmentation, and the Khwarazmian rise

entries.label: Tughril Beg — Founding the Sultanate
entries.hint: Tughril Beg led his Oghuz Turkic followers from Central Asia through Khorasan to Baghdad, where the Abbasid caliph invested him with the title Sultan in 1055 — the first time the caliphate formally recognised a single military ruler as supreme temporal authority over the whole Sunni Islamic world, ending the Buyid amirate in the same stroke.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, on Tughril Beg's entry into Baghdad and investiture.

entries.label: Alp Arslan — Manzikert
entries.hint: Alp Arslan's decisive defeat and capture of the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV Diogenes at Manzikert in 1071 shattered Byzantine defensive capacity in eastern Anatolia — opening the region to Turkic migration and settlement on a scale that would permanently reshape Anatolia's demographic and political future.
entries.note: Michael Attaleiates, History (Byzantine eyewitness account); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh.

entries.label: Malik-Shah I and Nizam al-Mulk
entries.hint: Malik-Shah's reign, guided for three decades by his formidable Persian vizier Nizam al-Mulk, marked the Seljuk sultanate's territorial and administrative peak — a partnership so effective that its end, with vizier and sultan both dead within weeks of each other in 1092, precipitated the sultanate's rapid fragmentation.
entries.note: Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, on the 1092 double death.

entries.label: The Fragmentation after Malik-Shah
entries.hint: Rival sons and regional atabegs (Turkic military guardians originally appointed to protect young Seljuk princes) carved the sultanate into competing power centres across Iran, Iraq and Syria — the atabegs increasingly ruling in their princely wards' names while accumulating genuinely independent authority of their own.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, on the succession wars following Malik-Shah's death.

entries.label: Sanjar — the Last Great Seljuk
entries.hint: Sanjar held the eastern Seljuk sultanate together from Merv for nearly four decades, the last ruler able to claim genuine authority over the dynasty's original Khorasan heartland, before Ghuzz Turkic tribesmen he had settled as frontier auxiliaries revolted, sacked Merv, and held him captive for several humiliating years until his death.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, on Sanjar's reign and captivity.

entries.label: The Khwarazmian Rise
entries.hint: Originally Seljuk-appointed governors of Khwarazm, the Khwarazm-Shahs expanded rapidly into the power vacuum left by Sanjar's death, briefly building an empire stretching across most of Iran and Central Asia — a state whose sudden vast extent and shallow administrative roots would prove catastrophically unable to withstand the Mongol invasion beginning in 1219.
entries.note: al-Nasawi, Sirat al-Sultan Jalal al-Din Mankubirti, on the rise of the Khwarazmian state.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Manzikert, the assassination of a great vizier, and Sanjar's captivity

entries.label: Tughril Beg Enters Baghdad
entries.hint: Tughril Beg's entry into Baghdad, ostensibly to rescue the caliph from a rebellious Turkic general, ended Buyid control of the city and installed the Seljuks as the new military power behind the Abbasid throne — a change of guard for the caliphate's protector-dynasty rather than any change in the caliph's own powerless status.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, on the Seljuk entry into Baghdad.

entries.label: The Battle of Manzikert
entries.hint: Alp Arslan's army defeated and captured the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV at Manzikert — treated with notable clemency by Alp Arslan himself — but the political chaos the defeat triggered at Constantinople did far more lasting damage to Byzantine Anatolia than the battle's own casualties, opening the region to unchecked Turkic migration for a generation afterward.
entries.note: Michael Attaleiates, History; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh.

entries.label: The Assassination of Nizam al-Mulk
entries.hint: A member of the Nizari Ismaili movement, disguised as a Sufi petitioner, stabbed Nizam al-Mulk to death — the first prominent victim of what would become a sustained Nizari campaign of targeted political killing, and a loss from which the Seljuk administrative machine never fully recovered.
entries.note: Rashid al-Din Hamadani, Jami al-Tawarikh, on the assassination and its attribution to the Nizaris.

entries.label: The Seljuk Succession Wars
entries.hint: Malik-Shah's sons and their atabeg guardians fought a prolonged, multi-sided civil war for control of the sultanate's core territories, permanently fracturing what had briefly been a unified Seljuk realm into the separate eastern (Khorasan) and western (Iraq-Iran) sultanates that would never again be reunited.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, on the succession wars of the 1090s and 1100s.

entries.label: The Ghuzz Revolt and Sanjar's Captivity
entries.hint: Ghuzz Turkic tribes Sanjar had settled as frontier guards in Khorasan revolted, defeated his army, and sacked Merv itself — one of the great cities of the Islamic world — before holding the aged sultan captive for roughly three years, a humiliating collapse of central authority from which the eastern Seljuk sultanate never recovered.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, on the Ghuzz revolt and the sack of Merv.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The Nizamiyya madrasas and the atabeg system of princely guardianship

entries.label: The Nizamiyya Madrasas
entries.hint: Nizam al-Mulk endowed a network of state-funded Sunni religious colleges (madrasas) across the sultanate's major cities, standardising advanced religious and legal education and training the administrators and jurists who staffed his own bureaucracy — an institutional model for state-sponsored higher education that spread across the wider Islamic world for centuries.
entries.note: Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama; George Makdisi, The Rise of Colleges (1981), on the Nizamiyya system.

entries.label: The Atabeg System
entries.hint: Turkic military commanders appointed as atabegs — guardians and tutors to young Seljuk princes given nominal provincial governorships — increasingly exercised the real power of the offices they formally only administered on a minor's behalf, a delegation of authority that repeatedly slid into outright independent atabeg dynasties across Iran, Iraq and Syria.
entries.note: Comparative institutional analysis of the Seljuk atabeg system and its successor states.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Sunni revival and the Nizari Ismaili state at Alamut

entries.label: The Nizari Ismaili State at Alamut
entries.hint: Hassan-i Sabbah seized the mountain fortress of Alamut in 1090 and built a network of similarly fortified strongholds into a genuinely independent Nizari Ismaili state within Seljuk territory, defended less by conventional armies than by a doctrine of targeted assassination of hostile political and religious leaders — the origin, via medieval European garbling of 'Hashishin,' of the English word 'assassin.'
entries.note: Rashid al-Din Hamadani, Jami al-Tawarikh; Marshall Hodgson, The Order of Assassins (1955).

entries.label: The Sunni Revival under Seljuk Patronage
entries.hint: Seljuk sultans and Nizam al-Mulk deliberately promoted Sunni orthodoxy — particularly through the Nizamiyya madrasas' curriculum — as an ideological counterweight to both the Shia Buyid legacy they had displaced and the Ismaili challenge growing at Alamut, a state-sponsored religious project as much political as theological in its aims.
entries.note: Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama, on the explicitly anti-Ismaili and pro-Sunni aims of his religious policy.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Great Mosque of Isfahan and Seljuk luster ceramics

entries.label: The Great Mosque of Isfahan's Dome Chambers
entries.hint: Nizam al-Mulk and his rival vizier Taj al-Mulk each sponsored one of two great brick dome chambers added to Isfahan's congregational mosque, their sophisticated squinch-and-muqarnas construction solving the geometric problem of setting a round dome over a square room with an elegance still studied by architectural historians as a high point of Islamic engineering.
entries.note: Masjed-e Jāmé of Isfahan, extant structure, UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 2012).

entries.label: Seljuk Luster Ceramics
entries.hint: Kashan's potters perfected a metallic luster-glaze technique producing pottery and tilework with a shimmering, almost metallic surface sheen — a technically demanding process requiring a second low-temperature firing that made Kashan wares prized luxury exports across the wider Islamic world.
entries.note: Seljuk-era Kashan luster ware corpus, Metropolitan Museum of Art and Victoria and Albert Museum.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Omar Khayyam, the Jalali calendar, and the Siyasatnama

entries.label: Omar Khayyam and the Jalali Calendar
entries.hint: Malik-Shah commissioned the poet-mathematician-astronomer Omar Khayyam to lead a team reforming the solar calendar, producing the Jalali calendar — more astronomically accurate over the long run than the Gregorian calendar that would not exist for another five centuries — while Khayyam's other work in algebra classified and solved cubic equations geometrically.
entries.note: Omar Khayyam's own astronomical and mathematical treatises; the Jalali calendar's continued partial use in modern Iran and Afghanistan.

entries.label: Nizam al-Mulk's Siyasatnama
entries.hint: Written for Malik-Shah near the end of his own life, the Siyasatnama ('Book of Government') laid out Nizam al-Mulk's theory of just and effective kingship through historical example and practical advice — one of the most influential works of Persian political theory, read and imitated by rulers and administrators for centuries after the Seljuk state it was written to serve had disappeared.
entries.note: Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama (Siyar al-Muluk).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Trade under a unified plateau and the wealth of Isfahan

entries.label: A Unified Plateau's Commercial Peak
entries.hint: Malik-Shah's reign briefly reunified nearly the whole Iranian plateau and much of the Fertile Crescent under a single political authority for the first time since the Abbasid caliphate's own early centuries — a political unity that measurably lowered the transaction costs of long-distance trade across a region more often divided among rival, mutually taxing powers.
entries.note: Comparative economic geography of the Great Seljuk sultanate at its territorial peak.

entries.label: The Iqta Land-Grant System
entries.hint: Seljuk administration relied heavily on iqta grants — assigning military commanders the tax revenue of a specified territory in lieu of a salary paid from the central treasury — a fiscal-military system that reduced the state's own cash-handling burden but steadily strengthened provincial commanders' independent power at the centre's expense.
entries.note: Ann Lambton, on the iqta system's development under the Great Seljuks.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The caravanserai network and Seljuk engineering

entries.label: The Caravanserai Network
entries.hint: Seljuk sultans and their viziers sponsored the construction of a dense network of fortified roadside inns (caravanserais) spaced roughly a day's journey apart across the plateau's major trade routes, dramatically improving the safety and speed of long-distance commercial and pilgrim travel.
entries.note: Surviving Seljuk-era caravanserai remains across the Iranian plateau; comparative infrastructure history.

entries.label: Kashan's Luster-Firing Technique
entries.hint: Producing luster ceramics required a precisely controlled second firing in a reducing (oxygen-starved) kiln atmosphere to deposit a thin metallic film on the glazed surface — a technically demanding process whose specific recipe Kashan's potter families guarded closely as valuable trade secrets.
entries.note: Technical ceramic analysis of Seljuk-era Kashan luster ware production methods.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Turkic settlement pouring into Anatolia after Manzikert

entries.label: Turkic Settlement Pours into Anatolia
entries.hint: In the decades following Manzikert, Turkic pastoralist tribes migrated into Anatolia in numbers far beyond what any single battle's aftermath could explain — a sustained demographic movement that would, over the following two centuries, transform Anatolia from a predominantly Greek Christian Byzantine province into the Turkish-speaking Muslim heartland from which the Ottoman Empire would eventually emerge.
entries.note: Speros Vryonis, The Decline of Medieval Hellenism in Asia Minor (1971), on the post-Manzikert Turkic settlement of Anatolia.

entries.label: Scholars Circulating through the Nizamiyya Network
entries.hint: The Nizamiyya madrasas at Baghdad, Nishapur, Isfahan and elsewhere formed a connected network across which scholars, texts and legal opinions moved with unusual freedom for the era — the theologian al-Ghazali's own career, teaching at the Baghdad Nizamiyya before a celebrated spiritual crisis and retreat, exemplifies the intellectual mobility the system enabled.
entries.note: al-Ghazali, al-Munqidh min al-Dalal (Deliverance from Error), on his own Nizamiyya teaching career.
